paragraphs.text: 1 Now it came to pass in the days of Ahasuerus, (this is Ahasuerus which reigned, from India even unto Ethiopia, over an hundred and seven and twenty provinces:) 2 That in those days, when the king Ahasuerus sat on the throne of his kingdom, which was in Shushan the palace, 3 In the third year of his reign, he made a feast unto all his princes and his servants; the power of Persia and Media, the nobles and princes of the provinces, being before him: 4 When he shewed the riches of his glorious kingdom and the honour of his excellent majesty many days, even an hundred and fourscore days. 5 And when these days were expired, the king made a feast unto all the people that were present in Shushan the palace, both unto great and small, seven days, in the court of the garden of the king’s palace; 6 Where were white, green, and blue, hangings, fastened with cords of fine linen and purple to silver rings and pillars of marble: the beds were of gold and silver, upon a pavement of alabaster, and marble, and pearl, and black marble. 7 And they gave them drink in vessels of gold, (the vessels being diverse one from another,) and royal wine in abundance, according to the state of the king. 8 And the drinking was according to the law; none did compel: for so the king had appointed to all the officers of his house, that they should do according to every man’s pleasure. 9 Also Vashti the queen made a feast for the women in the royal house which belonged to king Ahasuerus.

The kingdom of Media and Persia grew great and defeated the kingdom of Babylon, so the Jews who had been carried captive to Babylon came under Persian rule. The extent of this kingdom reached the point that it contained 127 provinces (states) stretching from India to Cush [1], that is, to Nubia and Kordofan, south of Egypt and north of Ethiopia. Among these provinces was the province of Egypt, which the emperor Xerxes occupied after his father had failed to seize it.

We have said that Ahasuerus [1] means King Xerxes the son of Darius. Since more than one king was given the title Ahasuerus, some scholars see that this word does not signify the king’s name but is a title special to the kings of Persia, like saying “Pharaoh” of the king of Egypt.

The king wanted to show the riches of the glory of his kingdom and the honour of the splendor of his majesty [4], so he made two great feasts. The first lasted 180 days; perhaps he held a daily feast for each province separately, together with special feasts for the princes as a body, or perhaps these cities covered the long period of preparing the two feasts. As for the second feast, [it was held for all the people, from great to small, a feast of seven days in the court of the garden of the king’s palace] [5].
Perhaps he prepared these two feasts in order to devise the plan of war against Greece, for Herodotus says that the Persians were accustomed to take their decisions at such feasts.

The book describes the feast in precise detail, mentioning that it was held in Shushan the palace. “Shushan,” or “Susa,” has been the capital of Elam since about the year 3000 B.C.; it was the seat of King Chedorlaomer (Gen 14:1). The kings of Media and Persia took possession of it and made it a capital alongside Babylon and Ecbatana, and the kings preferred to stay in it, especially in the winter. The first feast, for the princes, was apparently held inside the palace. The second, which included all the people residing in the palace and its dependencies (it seems it was separate from the city itself (Esth 9:12-13)), was held in the garden of the palace, where there were hangings (fabrics) of white, green and blue, which are the royal colors in Persia. These hangings were fastened with cords of fine linen (white linen) and purple to rings of silver and pillars of marble; the hangings were used for protection from the heat of the sun. The beds were inlaid with gold and silver upon a pavement, that is, a floor of tiles, of alabaster (a white stone that gleams), marble, pearl and black marble. The most notable feature of the feast was the drinking of the royal wine, which was found in abundance “according to the state of the king” [7], but he left the freedom of drinking to the choice of each person.
At the time when the king held this feast, the queen also held a feast for the women in the king’s house.

10 On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king, 11 To bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on. 12 But the queen Vashti refused to come at the king’s commandment by his chamberlains: therefore was the king very wroth, and his anger burned in him.

“On the seventh day, when the heart of the king was merry with wine, he commanded Mehuman, Biztha, Harbona, Bigtha, and Abagtha, Zethar, and Carcas, the seven chamberlains that served in the presence of Ahasuerus the king, to bring Vashti the queen before the king with the crown royal, to shew the people and the princes her beauty: for she was fair to look on” [10-11].

The king’s heart was merry with wine, so he lost his balance, and in foolishness he asked his seven chamberlains to bring the queen so that her beauty might be shown to the peoples and the princes. Here the word “eunuch” (chamberlain) does not carry its literal meaning, that is, a castrated man, but is a title that was given to the holders of royal offices in Egypt and Persia. Potiphar, the captain of the guard, was called “an officer of Pharaoh” (Gen 39:1), and so were the chief of Pharaoh’s cupbearers and his chief baker (Gen 40:2)... So the seven chamberlains are the men entrusted with the royal affairs, and they enjoy the favor of servants before the king.

The king’s heart was merry with wine, so he uttered perverse things, as the wise man says: “Look not thou upon the wine when it is red, when it giveth his colour in the cup, when it moveth itself aright. At the last it biteth like a serpent, and stingeth like an adder... thine heart shall utter perverse things” (Prov 23:31-33); “It is not for kings... to drink wine; nor for princes strong drink: lest they drink, and forget the law, and pervert the judgment of any of the afflicted” (Prov 31:4-5).

If in Christ Jesus we have become kings (Rev 1:6; 5:10), it is not fitting for us to become drunk with the wine of the love of this world and its pleasures, lest we forget the law of heaven and lose our fitting royal work, and demand the inner “Vashti” so that she may show her beauty before the peoples and the princes, that is, we present works of righteousness and virtues to gain human glory and for outward show, instead of our queen being within us, revealing her beauty only to her Bridegroom, our Lord Jesus!

If God has set man up as a spiritual king, then it is fitting for him not to demand his wife the queen in order to display her beauty, but to keep her in the house of the women, holding the feast for the women, so that they rejoice in her and submit to her. In other words, let our bodies (the wife) remain subject to the soul (the king), hidden in their royal conduct, living in a spirit of submission to the soul so as to remain holy in the Lord, sharing with the soul her glory and royal dignity. The Apostle Paul loved “Vashti,” that is, his royal body in the Lord, and left her in the house of the women, when he said: [I keep under my body, and bring it into subjection: lest that by any means, when I have preached to others, I myself should be a castaway] (1 Cor 9:27), “For no man ever yet hated his own flesh; but nourisheth and cherisheth it, even as the Lord the church,” that is, as a king toward the queen. Let the soul know its leading position by the Holy Spirit, and let the body know its position as a helper to the soul and a partner with her in victory, and the whole man is deprived of the eternal royal glory.

The king wanted to bring out the beauty of the queen “for she was fair to look on,” and he did not realize that by displaying her beauty she loses her dignity and her image is disfigured. For this reason our Lord Jesus affirmed our obligation not to display our inner queen, when He says: “Let not thy left hand know what thy right hand doeth: that thine alms may be in secret: and thy Father which seeth in secret himself shall reward thee openly” (Mt 6:3-4). Vashti remains in the house of the women when we offer worship to God not with the intent of appearing before people but by closing our inner doors and entering into the secret place, where we meet our unseen Bridegroom. As St. John Chrysostom says: [God Himself is unseen, therefore He wishes your prayer also to be unseen], and he also says: [God desires that the doors of the mind be shut rather than the (visible) doors].

entries.section: 3. Taking the kingdom away from Vashti:

paragraphs.text: 13 Then the king said to the wise men, which knew the times, (for so was the king’s manner toward all that knew law and judgment: 14 And the next unto him were Carshena, Shethar, Admatha, Tarshish, Meres, Marsena, and Memucan, the seven princes of Persia and Media, which saw the king’s face, and which sat the first in the kingdom;) 15 “What shall we do unto the queen Vashti according to law, because she hath not performed the commandment of the king Ahasuerus by the chamberlains?” 16 And Memucan answered before the king and the princes, “Vashti the queen hath not done wrong to the king only, but also to all the princes, and to all the people that are in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus. 17 For this deed of the queen shall come abroad unto all women, so that they shall despise their husbands in their eyes, when it shall be reported, The king Ahasuerus commanded Vashti the queen to be brought in before him, but she came not. 18 Likewise shall the ladies of Persia and Media say this day unto all the king’s princes, which have heard of the deed of the queen. Thus shall there arise too much contempt and wrath. 19 If it please the king, let there go a royal commandment from him, and let it be written among the laws of the Persians and the Medes, that it be not altered, That Vashti come no more before king Ahasuerus; and let the king give her royal estate unto another that is better than she. 20 And when the king’s decree which he shall make shall be published throughout all his empire, (for it is great,) all the wives shall give to their husbands honour, both to great and small.” 21 And the saying pleased the king and the princes; and the king did according to the word of Memucan: 22 For he sent letters into all the king’s provinces, into every province according to the writing thereof, and to every people after their language, that every man should bear rule in his own house, and that it should be published according to the language of every people.

When the queen refused to come, “the king was very wroth, and his anger burned in him” [12], and thus he turned to the opposite, from intense love and admiration for his wife the queen to flames of anger burning in him against her.

The king consulted the wise men who knew the times (perhaps meaning magicians and diviners) [13], and those who knew law and judgment... And since there seem to have been differences between the queen and Memucan, one of these counselors of the king, he exaggerated the matter and counted what Vashti had done as a wrong not only against the king and the princes but against all the men of his kingdom, for when the women hear what happened they will despise their husbands. And he asked that the kingdom be taken away from her and given to one who is better than she [19].

Memucan counted Vashti’s conduct as a breach of the law of nature and the law of the family, whereby the man loses his authority over his wife and the wife despises her husband, and he thought that it is laws that support the man and give him authority. Perhaps this conduct reveals an inner feeling that was passing through the lives of men in that age, namely the inability to control and lead the family; they did not realize that wise leadership does not draw its strength from laws and commands but from a spirit of self-giving love, as the Apostle says: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it... Nevertheless let every one of you in particular so love his wife even as himself” (Eph 5:25, 33).

entries.section: 3. Taking the kingdom away from Vashti:

paragraphs.text: Memucan says: “that every man should bear rule in his own house, and that it should be published according to the language of every people” [22], meaning that if a man marries a woman of another race, the household is obliged to speak the language of the man and not the woman. This is the picture of family life in the minds of the men of Persia, and they did not realize that the language that prevails in the home must be the language of love, which is able to captivate the beloved. Between wife and husband there is no struggle for authority; rather there ought to be between them a longing for self-giving that works through inner love, and an awareness of the unity of life and thought.

Ahasuerus loved Vashti for her beauty, her lineage and her wealth, and in his anger he took counsel with others about her. We, however, receive the wife (or the husband) from the hand of God, that He may grant us the spirit of unity in Him, sanctifying the family relationship which cannot be dissolved. As Tertullian says: [How can I describe the happiness of the marriage that the Church approves, the offering confirms, the blessing seals, the angels announce, and the Father declares lawful?!].

entries.section: 1. The need for a new queen:

paragraphs.text: 1 After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. 2 Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, “Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: 3 And let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king’s chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: 4 And let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti.” And the thing pleased the king; and he did so.

“After these things, when the wrath of king Ahasuerus was appeased, he remembered Vashti, and what she had done, and what was decreed against her. Then said the king’s servants that ministered unto him, Let there be fair young virgins sought for the king: and let the king appoint officers in all the provinces of his kingdom, that they may gather together all the fair young virgins unto Shushan the palace, to the house of the women, unto the custody of Hege the king’s chamberlain, keeper of the women; and let their things for purification be given them: and let the maiden which pleaseth the king be queen instead of Vashti” [1-3].

The king’s wrath was appeased and he remembered Vashti, and perhaps he could have pardoned her, but the counselors feared lest she take vengeance on them because of their counsel to the king, so they hastened to urge him to choose a beautiful wife. It is said that the king used to choose his wife from the daughters of the princes, but since the men feared that the king would think they had pushed him to dismiss Vashti for a personal interest, they tried to show their good intention by having the king choose the beautiful maiden from any province or any race, as they would gather for him the fair maidens from the whole kingdom. By this they wanted to offer a remedy for the dismissal of Vashti by installing a beautiful woman in her place. As St. Jerome says: [The philosophers of the world used to remove an old passion by instilling a new passion, driving out one nail by fixing another. On this basis the seven princes of Persia acted with King Ahasuerus, for they removed his regret over Vashti the queen by stirring up in him love for other virgins. They heal one fault with another, and one sin with another sin; but for us it is fitting to overcome our faults by teaching ourselves the love of the opposite virtues. As the psalmist says: “Depart from evil, and do good; seek peace, and pursue it” (Ps 34:14). For if we do not hate evil we cannot love good; rather let us do good if we wish to leave evil; let us seek peace if we wish to avoid war.]

The princes exploited the weakness of the king’s character and his love of licentiousness, so they quenched his longing for Vashti by offering beautiful maidens to the house of the women, that he might choose according to his desire.

If we take the symbolic or spiritual interpretation, we ask: who are these servants who minister to him and ask him to set up a new queen instead of Vashti, if not the men of faith of the Old Testament, patriarchs, prophets, kings, priests and laymen, who lived under the shadow of the Law (Vashti), and realized that there is no salvation for them by the Law, especially in its literalness, since “the commandment (the Law), which was ordained to life, I found to be unto death. For sin, taking occasion by the commandment, deceived me, and by it slew me” (Rom 7:10-11). The Law exposed sin and disgraced it (Rom 7:12) and confirmed the death of man instead of supporting, healing and saving him. For this reason the men of the Old Testament awaited with joy the coming of the “Messiah,” the Savior, to set up Esther as queen through the free grace of the Gospel, as the Lord Himself says: “Your father Abraham rejoiced to see my day: and he saw it, and was glad” (Jn 8:56).

The servants asked that the fair young virgins be gathered from the whole kingdom to Shushan the palace, as if they, the men of the Old Testament, saw the Church of the New Testament, which has included in its membership children from all the nations and peoples, and has entered with them into the house of the virgins in the palace of Christ, that is, the Church which is called “the church of the firstborn” (Heb 12:23), to declare her spiritual virginity and her inner beauty as “a glorious church, not having spot, or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and without blemish” (Eph 5:27). The believers longed to see this holy virgin as a bride for the King, as the Apostle Paul says: “For I have espoused you to one husband, that I may present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor 11:2).

5 Now in Shushan the palace there was a certain Jew, whose name was Mordecai, the son of Jair, the son of Shimei, the son of Kish, a Benjamite; 6 Who had been carried away from Jerusalem with the captivity which had been carried away with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away. 7 And he brought up Hadassah, that is, Esther, his uncle’s daughter: for she had neither father nor mother, and the maid was fair and beautiful; whom Mordecai, when her father and mother were dead, took for his own daughter. 8 So it came to pass, when the king’s commandment and his decree was heard, and when many maidens were gathered together unto Shushan the palace, to the custody of Hegai, that Esther was brought also unto the king’s house, to the custody of Hegai, keeper of the women. 9 And the maiden pleased him, and she obtained kindness of him; and he speedily gave her her things for purification, with such things as belonged to her, and seven maidens, which were meet to be given her, out of the king’s house: and he preferred her and her maids unto the best place of the house of the women. 10 Esther had not shewed her people nor her kindred: for Mordecai had charged her that she should not shew it. 11 And Mordecai walked every day before the court of the women’s house, to know how Esther did, and what should become of her.

When Vashti was removed from the kingdom, God turned this matter to the salvation of His people by raising up Esther, who was born in the land of captivity and was brought up by her cousin Mordecai, as queen instead of Vashti.

The book speaks of Mordecai, who worked in Shushan the palace; he was a Jew carried away from Jerusalem in the days of Jeconiah king of Judah by Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon. What draws our attention is that the hidden hero in the story of Esther is “Mordecai,” who was marked by faithfulness in raising Esther and in his guidance to her, and by faithfulness in his work for the king, who was of a foreign race, saving his life from a wicked plot; he was also distinguished by a deeply spiritual conduct filled with faith and trust in the work of God.

We have said that Vashti signifies the literalness of the Law, which must be removed from the heart so that the grace of the New Testament may reign, and Esther (the Church of the New Testament) appears as queen. The features and circumstances of Esther came in conformity with the Church of the New Testament in many respects, of which we mention:

First: Esther was born in the land of captivity, deprived of the Promised Land and of the Temple with all its beautiful rituals, as if she represents the company of the Gentiles who fell under the captivity of the devil, deprived of God’s spiritual blessings and of the enjoyment of His temple... But God raised them from this captivity and made them spiritual kings, for the Lord Christ came to set them free, as it is said by Isaiah: “He hath sent me to bind up the brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to them that are bound” (Isa 61:1).

St. Augustine says: [Our captivity was removed, not by our being freed from the hands of the barbarians... but from our evil works and from our sins by which the devil had dominion over us; whoever is freed from his sins, the chief of sinners (the devil) no longer has dominion over him], and he also says: [Confess that you are a captive and you will deserve to be freed; for he who does not know his enemy, how can he urge on his deliverer?].

Second: “she had neither father nor mother” [7], that is, she was an orphan. This is the mark of the Church when she fulfilled God’s call to Abraham: “Get thee... from thy father’s house” (Gen 12:1). Let us leave our old father, the devil, and our first mother, that is, the love of the world, so that the Lord Himself may be our heavenly Father and the heavenly Church our mother. The Lord asked the Jews to become orphans of their evil father when He said to them: “Ye are of your father the devil, and the lusts of your father ye will do” (Jn 8:44). And St. Augustine speaks about the Gentiles’ leaving their old father, saying: [The Gentiles came from their father Satan and renounced their sonship to him].

Third: “the maid was fair and beautiful” [7]... The heavenly Bridegroom sees in His bride the queen a beauty that He Himself poured upon her, for He says to her: “And thy renown went forth among the heathen for thy beauty: for it was perfect through my comeliness, which I had put upon thee, saith the Lord GOD” (Ezek 16:14). Though our past was disgraced by the blackness of sin, yet with exultation we say: “I am black, but comely, O ye daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 1:5). And as St. Ambrose says: [Since you put on those garments through the font of Baptism, you say in the Song of Songs, “I am black, but comely (perfect), O ye daughters of Jerusalem.” I am black through human weakness, perfect through the mystery of faith].
Fourth: “(Hegai) moved her with her maids to the best place in the house of the women, and Esther did not tell of her people and her kindred” [9-10].

Hegai was the keeper of the house of the virgins, and Shaashgaz the keeper of the concubines [14]. As for Esther, she entered the house of the virgins and was placed in the best place in it, for he realized that she would find favour in the sight of the king and be made queen. What is this place if not “sonship to God,” which became ours as the gift of the Holy Spirit to us in Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son? For in Him we have been raised into the bosom of His Father, to be found with Him as sons of His.

Esther did not tell of her people and her kindred, as Mordecai counseled. For the soul, when it enjoys sonship to God and becomes a queen, lives on a heavenly level, and it has a transcendent race that language cannot express. She lives in silence, not the silence of helplessness grounded in the closing of the heart, but the silence of love opened toward heaven, contemplating the works of God with a glorious joy that cannot be spoken.

Fifth: her humility. Esther was marked by a spirit of obedience and submission to her foster father Mordecai even after she sat as queen on the greatest throne of that time, for it is said: “for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him” [20].

12 Now when every maid’s turn was come to go in to king Ahasuerus, after that she had been twelve months, according to the manner of the women, (for so were the days of their purifications accomplished, to wit, six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with other things for the purifying of the women;) 13 Then thus came every maiden unto the king; whatsoever she desired was given her to go with her out of the house of the women unto the king’s house. 14 In the evening she went, and on the morrow she returned into the second house of the women, to the custody of Shaashgaz, the king’s chamberlain, which kept the concubines: she came in unto the king no more, except the king delighted in her, and that she were called by name. 15 Now when the turn of Esther, the daughter of Abihail the uncle of Mordecai, who had taken her for his daughter, was come to go in unto the king, she required nothing but what Hegai the king’s chamberlain, the keeper of the women, appointed. And Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her. 16 So Esther was taken unto king Ahasuerus into his house royal in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign. 17 And the king loved Esther above all the women, and she obtained grace and favour in his sight more than all the virgins; so that he set the royal crown upon her head, and made her queen instead of Vashti. 18 Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king. 19 And when the virgins were gathered together the second time, then Mordecai sat in the king’s gate. 20 Esther had not yet shewed her kindred nor her people; as Mordecai had charged her: for Esther did the commandment of Mordecai, like as when she was brought up with him.

When Xerxes returned defeated from his campaign against Greece, he busied himself with choosing the new queen, and it seems that what was done by way of preparations with the virgins took place before his coming from the battle and not after his coming, since the virgins remained a whole year preparing for the meeting with the king. And the book relates to us the preparations that were made for Esther, which are:

First: the days of her purification were completed, “six months with oil of myrrh, and six months with sweet odours, and with other things for the purifying of the women” [12]. What do the six months in which she was perfumed with oil of myrrh mean if not her acceptance of burial with her Bridegroom Christ, who was buried after being anointed with myrrh... She remains six months, and the number 6 signifies the days of creation, that is, she remains bearing sufferings and being buried with her Bridegroom all the days of her sojourn until her spiritual perfection is completed and she meets the Lord face to face on the seventh day. And as she is buried with the Lord, so she rises with Him, for the sweet odours and the ointments signify the joyous fragrance of the resurrection. Therefore let us suffer with Him, be buried with Him, and also rise with Him! This is the way to reach the heavenly crown. As St. John Chrysostom says: [It is fitting for you that these sufferings not trouble you but rather rejoice you... Thus it is fitting for us to walk the way so that we may share with Him in glory and honor... How glorious are the sufferings! By them we are conformed to His death!].

Second: “whatsoever she desired was given her to go with her out of the house of the women unto the king’s house” [13]. The virgin carries with her all that she wants from the house of the women (the virgins), for as she sets out to her Bridegroom the heavenly King, she carries what she has gathered here of holy things such as love, purity and heavenly thought. She carries it as a sign of love for her Bridegroom, from what He Himself gave her during the days of her sojourn on earth, that is, she offers to Him from what He gave her.

Third: “Esther obtained favour in the sight of all them that looked upon her” [15]. This is her true asset: the free grace of God, which raises the soul and lifts her until she is fit for a kingdom (Ezek 16:13), so that she finds favour in the eyes of all... This is the grace of God that upholds man in his striving, of which St. John Chrysostom said: [None is stronger than he who enjoys heavenly help, as none is weaker than he who is deprived of it].

Fourth: “Esther was taken... in the tenth month, which is the month Tebeth, in the seventh year of his reign” [16]. Esther could be set up as queen only in the tenth month in the seventh year. The tenth month signifies the fulfillment of the Law (10 commandments), which is accomplished through our union in Christ, who alone did not break the Law, while the seventh year signifies the perfection of the Gospel. It is as though our enjoyment of the Kingdom is realized by our receiving the Law spiritually in the Lord through the grace of the Gospel.

Fifth: “Then the king made a great feast unto all his princes and his servants, even Esther’s feast; and he made a release to the provinces, and gave gifts, according to the state of the king” [18]. Esther made him forget the troubles of his battle with Greece and his heavy loss, and his life was turned into joy, as he gave rest to the land, that is, exemption from tribute for a year or exemption from conscription...

The king put the crown with his own hands on her head [17], for the soul cannot reign except through Christ Jesus, who crowns her with the crown of His glory, and makes a feast in her name that gladdens the heart of the heavenly ones. And it is a rest, for the Lord counts her crown a blessed Sabbath and a joyous feast. As for His gifts, which are according to the king’s generosity, they are the giving of Himself to us as a Bridegroom whom we carry within us. He is the Giver and the gift; He does not withhold Himself from us but with joy receives us, that we may say: “My beloved is mine, and I am his: he feedeth among the lilies” (Song 2:16). And as St. Augustine addresses Him, saying: [You watch over me, as though You had forgotten all creation! You give me Your gifts, as if I alone were the object of Your love].

21 In those days, while Mordecai sat in the king’s gate, two of the king’s chamberlains, Bigthan and Teresh, of those which kept the door, were wroth, and sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. 22 And the thing was known to Mordecai, who told it unto Esther the queen; and Esther certified the king thereof in Mordecai’s name. 23 And when inquisition was made of the matter, it was found out; therefore they were both hanged on a tree: and it was written in the book of the chronicles before the king.
Mordecai was marked by faithfulness. He was faithful in his private life, as in his raising of Esther, and in his service to the king, as in his love for his people.

Mordecai learned that two chamberlains, keepers of the door, were plotting to assassinate the king, so he told Esther, who told the king. And when the king examined the matter and verified it, he hanged them on a tree, and the matter was written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of the Persians.

In (the Additions to Esth 12:4-5) it relates to us that the king gave gifts to Mordecai, but afterwards, when sleep fled from the king and he read what had been written earlier, he counted what Mordecai had received as nothing (Esth 6:1-11), and wanted to honor him in an extraordinary way. We also, when we strive here for the salvation of our brethren from eternal punishment, the Lord counts it as a debt, although He is the One working in us and with us, and so grants us blessings and graces; but all this He counts as nothing when He crowns us with the crown of eternal life and brings us into the fellowship of His glories, to live with Him face to face in the bosom of the Father.

entries.section: 1. The king recalls the deeds of Mordecai:

paragraphs.text: "1 On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king. 2 And it was found written, that Mordecai had told of Bigthana and Teresh, two of the king's chamberlains, the keepers of the door, who sought to lay hand on the king Ahasuerus. 3 And the king said, What honour and dignity hath been done to Mordecai for this? Then said the king's servants that ministered unto him, There is nothing done for him." [1-3].

What a wonderful timing! While Esther was preparing the banquet, and it was not easy for her to attack Haman, the king's favorite, and while Haman was spending the whole night preparing a huge cross for Mordecai, God was using all the events together to accomplish His plan of salvation in the most wonderful way. What Mordecai and Esther could not do, the Lord Himself did, taking sleep from the king's eyes so that He might urge him to reward Mordecai for his faithfulness in his work and for saving his life.

Here it is fitting for us to pause a little and see the prayers of Mordecai answered at the proper time. When I say his prayers, I do not mean merely the outward words from his mouth, but his whole life. For every spiritual work, every act of faithfulness and every sanctification turns our life into prayers accepted before God. What Mordecai did years ago, when he served the king faithfully and saved him from the wicked plot, was a prayer to God Himself, who accepts every spiritual work and every act of faithfulness as the fragrance of sweet incense. By this we understand the saying of the Psalmist: "But I am prayer" (Ps 109:4), realizing that every member of our body, every emotion and every feeling, when sanctified and striving in the Lord, becomes like an active tongue that opens the gates of heaven to bring us into the presence of God. "The effectual fervent prayer of a righteous man availeth much" (Jas 5:16), because what his tongue utters in petitions comes forth in harmony with what his whole life proclaims, being itself a prayer. On the contrary, the prayer of the wicked is an abomination before the Lord, because he utters one thing while his life utters another, so that it becomes a discord in which the Lord finds no rest.

The Lord answered the prayers of Mordecai, which he offered by his practical life as well as by his tongue. While Haman was perfecting his plan to bring Mordecai down to the dust, behold, God "raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth up the beggar from the dunghill, to set them among princes, and to make them inherit the throne of glory: for the pillars of the earth are the LORD'S" (1 Sam 2:8).

Sleep fled from the king's eyes, and when he remembered the deeds of Mordecai and asked about his reward, according to what he had received, it was nothing, and his heart had no rest until he returned love for love. He realized that Mordecai had saved his life, so what reward would be fitting for such a deed? Truly, if this was the feeling of a king known for his cruelty, what is fitting for us to render to God in return for His love, since He saved us from our deadly sins? As St. John Chrysostom says: [If Mordecai, when the king remembered his services, found them profitable to him and was raised by them to such great glory, how much more does it befit us to be thankful to God and to offer Him abundantly all that we have, when we remember His forgiveness of the sins we committed against Him and the goodness He has shown us!].

4 And the king said, Who is in the court? Now Haman was come into the outward court of the king's house, to speak unto the king to hang Mordecai on the gallows that he had prepared for him. 5 And the king's servants said unto him, Behold, Haman standeth in the court. And the king said, Let him come in. 6 So Haman came in. And the king said unto him, What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself? 7 And Haman answered the king, For the man whom the king delighteth to honour, 8 Let the royal apparel be brought which the king useth to wear, and the horse that the king rideth upon, and the crown royal which is set upon his head: 9 And let this apparel and horse be delivered to the hand of one of the king's most noble princes, that they may array the man withal whom the king delighteth to honour, and bring him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaim before him, Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

Haman came early in the morning, after a night that he perhaps spent entirely with the carpenters building the cross. He wished to meet the king to ask his permission to hang Mordecai, so that he might enjoy inner peace before delighting in Esther's banquet. Instead he found the king himself asking for him in order to consult him, saying to him: "What shall be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour? Now Haman thought in his heart, To whom would the king delight to do honour more than to myself?" [6]. In the pride of his heart he thought that there was no man whom the king loved as he did, so he exaggerated the honor greatly, not realizing that "Pride goeth before destruction, and an haughty spirit before a fall" (Prov 16:18), and that "When pride cometh, then cometh shame: but with the lowly is wisdom" (Prov 11:2). As the Father Mar Isaac the Syrian says: [Worldly glory is like a rock hidden in the sea; the sailor does not know it until a ship strikes it, its bottom is torn and it fills with water].

He exaggerated the honor and asked that the one loved by the king be clothed with the royal robe and ride the king's horse, with a crown set on the horse's head, as was the custom of the Assyrians and the Persians, and that it be proclaimed before him in the square of the city: Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

Haman carried the spirit of the devil, whom God honored before his fall, so that he was a cherub with the highest of the heavenly orders, and who in pride wanted to seize for himself what belongs to God. In the same way Haman wanted to seize the king's robe, his horse and his honor!

10 Then the king said to Haman, Make haste, and take the apparel and the horse, as thou hast said, and do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king's gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken. 11 Then took Haman the apparel and the horse, and arrayed Mordecai, and brought him on horseback through the street of the city, and proclaimed before him, Thus shall it be done unto the man whom the king delighteth to honour.

The words of the king fell on Haman's ears like a thunderbolt when he said to him: "Do even so to Mordecai the Jew, that sitteth at the king's gate: let nothing fail of all that thou hast spoken" [10]. If Haman could not bear Mordecai because of his nationality and his belonging to God, here is the king glorifying and honoring him, calling him "the Jew", and perhaps he learned this during his discussion about his reward.

How wonderful! Mordecai humbled himself, so the king raised him to surpassing honor, and Haman's heart exalted itself, so he fell beneath his feet. Because of Mordecai's humility he was raised in order to save their lives and to turn the dark day of their destruction into the joyful feast of Purim, whereas Haman, encouraged by his loved ones, became proud, fell and perished with his sons and all his family.

What do we see in the glorified Mordecai but the work of the glorified Christ, who raised us with Him to His glory after He humbled Himself for our sake and cried out on the Cross because of us with a bitter cry? Mordecai put on the royal robe, but the Lord Christ gave us Himself that we might put Him on (Gal 3:27) and be hidden in Him. Mordecai rode a royal horse, but the Lord Christ granted us His divine grace to carry us from glory to glory and bring us to the bosom of His Father. Mordecai received the king's crown, but the Lord Christ granted us in Him the partaking of the divine nature and made us heirs of God and joint-heirs with Christ (Rom 8:17); in Him we became the object of the Father's pleasure, and it was proclaimed before us: [Thus shall it be done to the man whom the king delighteth to honour].

As much as Mordecai was glorified, Haman fell before him until he was under his feet. As the Father Aphrahat says: [Mordecai trod on the neck of Haman his persecutor, and Jesus trampled on His enemies with His feet].

12 And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered. 13 And Haman told Zeresh his wife and all his friends every thing that had befallen him. Then said his wise men and Zeresh his wife unto him, If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him. 14 And while they were yet talking with him, came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared.
"And Mordecai came again to the king's gate. But Haman hasted to his house mourning, and having his head covered" [12].

When Mordecai was honored in the square of the city and received a glory that no one had expected, he returned to the king's house with head held high, but Haman, to whom all used to bow, was ashamed and returned to his house mourning and with his head covered. For a man, covering the head was a sign of intense grief and shame. When David fled from before his son Absalom, "he went up... weeping as he went up, and had his head covered, and he went barefoot: and all the people that was with him covered every man his head" (2 Sam 15:30). And when the nobles of Judah were put to shame because of the severe drought and their return from the pits with empty vessels, they covered their heads (Jer 14:3).

At any rate, Mordecai returned to the king's house as though it were his own house, since the king had declared him to be beloved to him, and Haman returned to his house full of disgrace and shame. It is as though Mordecai points to the soul glorified in the Lord, victorious by the Holy Spirit, which departs to heaven, "the king's house", as though it were its own house and special dwelling place, whereas the wicked soul that falls like Haman does not return to the life of Paradise but hastens to its own house, that is, to the "ego", and lives shut up in itself, full of grief and shame. It lives with a covering on its head, placing a veil over its mind so that it does not go forth to see the divine things, to behold the heavens and to swim in the eternal realities.

Haman returned to his house to meet with Zeresh his wife and his wise men (the sorcerers), who announced his fall to him and thereby crushed his soul even more, for they said to him: "If Mordecai be of the seed of the Jews, before whom thou hast begun to fall, thou shalt not prevail against him, but shalt surely fall before him..." [13]. Perhaps they prophesied to him what would come upon him, or perhaps they realized that what they had been dreaming of all night had been turned upside down, and that this could not be mere chance but was accomplished by a mighty hidden hand. Here they felt that what had happened that day was only the beginning of Haman's collapse and of a fall that would continue to the end, so they could not offer him a word of encouragement or hope.

It seems that these words crushed him so that he became slow to go to Esther's banquet, for it is said: "And while they were yet talking with him, came the king's chamberlains, and hasted to bring Haman unto the banquet that Esther had prepared" [14].

Haman went out to the banquet in a spirit different from the one in which he had received the invitation the day before, for he became like a sheep led to the slaughter. Truly, [it is a fearful thing to fall into the hands of the living God] (Heb 10:31), and as the Psalmist says: "The heathen are sunk down in the pit that they made: in the net which they hid is their own foot taken. The LORD is known by the judgment which he executeth: the wicked is snared in the work of his own hands" (Ps 9:15-16).
"So the king and Haman came to banquet with Esther the queen." [1].

What is this banquet that Esther prepared, at which the king and Haman were to drink, but the banquet of the Cross, which the Church offers to the King, that is, to God, who is pleased with the sacrifice of the Savior and smells it as a sweet savor? Therefore the priest prays: "He who offered Himself as an acceptable sacrifice on the Cross for the salvation of our race, and His good Father smelled it in the evening on Golgotha."

If the King drank with joy at the banquet of the Cross and smelled the fragrance of the love of His beloved Son, Haman drank at the same banquet the cup of God's wrath upon him and upon his wicked works. The banquet that gladdened the heart of God with His Church crushed the devil, exposed his deceptions and removed his authority.

2 And the king said again unto Esther on the second day at the banquet of wine, What is thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? and it shall be performed, even to the half of the kingdom. 3 Then Esther the queen answered and said, If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: 4 For we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage.

When the king entered the banquet and drank out of Esther's love for him, he said to her: "What is thy petition, queen Esther? and it shall be granted thee: and what is thy request? and it shall be performed, even to the half of the kingdom" [2]. He calls her by her name and asks her to request even up to half of his kingdom, since he regarded her as his own, his partner in his glory. At the same time he calls her "the queen" to remind her of her royal position, so that she has the right to ask with boldness and confidence, and so to win the king's heart and his glory as well.

These are the feelings and words of God to every soul. He calls it by its name as His own special bride, and calls it queen so that it may come to the throne of His grace with confidence (Heb 4:16), and He asks it to gladden His heart by asking Him to take even up to half of His kingdom. Therefore the Lord urges His disciples: "Hitherto have ye asked nothing in my name: ask, and ye shall receive, that your joy may be full" (Jn 16:24).

God longs for every soul to ask Him so that it may receive, for He desires to give it even Himself and to make it an heir enjoying the partaking of His glories. In the face of this surpassing divine love, what does the Church ask, or the human soul as a member of the Church? Like Esther, it asks for neither money nor honor nor any earthly blessing, but it asks for the salvation of its own soul and the salvation of its brethren, for she said: "If I have found favour in thy sight, O king, and if it please the king, let my life be given me at my petition, and my people at my request: for we are sold, I and my people, to be destroyed, to be slain, and to perish. But if we had been sold for bondmen and bondwomen, I had held my tongue, although the enemy could not countervail the king's damage" [3-5].
What does Esther ask, when her life and the life of her people were exposed to destruction, slaughter and extermination?!

Here Esther stands out as a true mother who embraces all her brethren with love, working and asking for the salvation of all. She did not stand passive before her brethren, but humbled herself, prayed and struggled to the end for their salvation. For the life of faith leads a person out of the ego to live with an open mouth and a heart enlarged for all (2 Cor 6:11). This is what the Apostle declared when he said: "O ye Corinthians, our mouth is open unto you, our heart is enlarged... Now for a recompense in the same, (I speak as unto my children,) be ye also enlarged" (2 Cor 6:11, 13). In the same spirit St. John Chrysostom says: [Nothing makes a person so like Christ as his care for his neighbor], [I cannot believe that a person who does not work for the salvation of his brother is saved], [Nothing is so worthless as a Christian who does not care for the salvation of others... Everyone can help his brother, even if only with good will, if it is not within his power to do anything... If you say that you are a Christian and cannot do anything for others, there is a contradiction in what you say, as if one were to say that the sun cannot give light].

5 Then the king Ahasuerus answered and said unto Esther the queen, Who is he, and where is he, that durst presume in his heart to do so? 6 And Esther said, The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen.

When the king asked about the enemy who had sold Esther and her people to destruction, slaughter and extermination, she said: "The adversary and enemy is this wicked Haman. Then Haman was afraid before the king and the queen" [6].

If the first work of the banquet of the Cross is the salvation of Esther (the Church) and her people, this will be accomplished only through the exposure of wicked Haman and his loss of all authority, so that he stands terrified before God and the holy Church. As St. Paul says: "Having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it" (that is, in the Cross) (Col 2:15). St. John Chrysostom speaks about the Cross, saying: [By it the demons are no longer terrifying but worthless and despised. By it death is no longer death but sleep, for the one who fights us has been cast under our feet].

entries.section: 4. The humiliation of Haman before Esther:

paragraphs.text: 7 And the king arising from the banquet of wine in his wrath went into the palace garden: and Haman stood up to make request for his life to Esther the queen; for he saw that there was evil determined against him by the king. 8 Then the king returned out of the palace garden into the place of the banquet of wine; and Haman was fallen upon the bed whereon Esther was. Then said the king, Will he force the queen also before me in the house? As the word went out of king's mouth, they covered Haman's face.

entries.section: 4. The humiliation of Haman before Esther:

paragraphs.text: If the Cross exposed Satan, broke his power and destroyed the death that he brought upon man, so that he was cast down under the feet of the Savior, then he has entered into humiliation before the human being who reigns without him. This meaning was revealed in the fall of Haman at the feet of Esther, who was sitting on the bed, according to the custom of the East in ancient times at banquets... And since the king had gone out into the palace garden, perhaps to think what to do, he returned and found Haman thus in humiliation, entreating while fallen upon the bed, and said: "Will he force the queen also before me in the house?!" [8]. He did not suspect anything, for he knew the bitterness of Haman's soul at that moment, but these words of his came to express his inward fury... They were a sign to those standing by of the king's wrath and put an end to Haman's life.

What the king said: "Will he force the queen also before me in the house?!" declares God's view of the true Haman, that is, the devil, who enters the heart of the believer to seize the soul from the hand and bosom of God, as though he were Haman who wished to draw Esther away from the king's bosom and violate her! God is a jealous God; He cannot bear that the enemy should enter His house and snatch His bride from between His hands!

9 And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon. 10 So they hanged Haman on the gallows that he had prepared for Mordecai. Then was the king's wrath pacified.

When he declared his anger against Haman, "they covered Haman's face. And Harbonah, one of the chamberlains, said before the king, Behold also, the gallows fifty cubits high, which Haman had made for Mordecai, who had spoken good for the king, standeth in the house of Haman. Then the king said, Hang him thereon" [8-10].

Thus Haman was justly hanged on the very gallows that he had prepared unjustly for Mordecai, as it is said: "The righteous is delivered out of trouble, and the wicked cometh in his stead" (Prov 11:8), "The wicked shall be a ransom for the righteous, and the transgressor for the upright" (Prov 21:18), "The wicked is snared in the work of his own hands... in the net which they hid is their own foot taken" (Ps 9:16, 15). "As thou hast done, it shall be done unto thee: thy reward shall return upon thine own head" (Obad 15), "With what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again" (Mt 7:2).

Satan rejoiced over the Cross and stirred up his helpers to accomplish it, and did not realize that what he was doing would return upon him. As St. Jerome says: [On the Cross Satan and all his host were put to shame; Christ was certainly crucified in the body, and behold, He crucifies the demons on the Cross].

entries.section: 1. Esther and the house of Haman:

paragraphs.text: 1 On that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman the Jews' enemy unto Esther the queen. And Mordecai came before the king; for Esther had told what he was unto her.
"On that day did the king Ahasuerus give the house of Haman the Jews' enemy unto Esther the queen" [1].

Haman had asked his helpers to cast lots to determine a day on which Haman would inherit all that belonged to the Jews after killing them, yet behold, Haman was delivered to death, and the king gave his house into the hands of Esther the Jewess.

If the true Haman, the devil, set in his heart to seize the heart of man and inherit it after crushing and destroying it, then through the banquet of the Cross man took the position that Satan held before his fall, and became as one who has entered into the heavenly orders as one of them. Some of the Fathers see that the heavenly orders are seven, besides the Cherubim and Seraphim, and man has become like the tenth order in place of the devil, who was the morning star standing in the presence of God. The enemy fell into the abyss so that man might rise, be lifted up to heaven and reign in the place of the fallen enemy!

If Satan set himself up as the ruler of this world by the enticements of sin (Jn 12:31), seizing the house of man which God gave us to dwell in with authority, then through the banquet of the Cross man not only recovered his house but was raised with the Lord to Paradise. In this connection St. Gregory of Nyssa addresses the candidates for baptism, saying: [You are outside Paradise, O catechumens. You share with Adam your first father in his exile. But now the door is opened and you return to where you came out].

The feast of Purim is the feast of the annulment of Haman's lot for the destruction of the believers, so that the Lord may declare that they are His portion, heirs of the house of the fallen enemy, and enjoying entrance into heaven itself.
2 And the king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it unto Mordecai. And Esther set Mordecai over the house of Haman.
"And the king took off his ring, which he had taken from Haman, and gave it unto Mordecai" [2].

When the prodigal son returned to his father, the father said: "Put a ring on his hand" (Lk 15:22), a sign of true sonship and a confirmation of his filial authority. So the believer, Mordecai, enjoys the king's ring, as the Evangelist says: "As many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God, even to them that believe on his name: which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God" (Jn 1:12-13). This is the royal ring, the "filial authority" which we receive by the Holy Spirit in the waters of Baptism. For this reason many Fathers spoke of Baptism as a seal on the soul, such as St. Clement of Rome, Hermas, Tertullian and St. John Chrysostom. St. Augustine says of this seal: [Hold fast to what you have received, for it will not change; it is a royal mark]. By this seal we enter into the possession of God, as the Father Theodore of Mopsuestia says: [The sign with which you are now marked is a sign that you have become the flock of Christ]. By this seal we also enter into spiritual soldiery, and as St. Cyril of Jerusalem says: [Each one of you comes and presents himself before God, in the presence of countless armies of angels, and the Holy Spirit sets a mark upon your souls. By this you enroll yourselves in the army of the great King].

By this seal, as we enjoy the authority of sonship and live in the possession of God as His children, and live as spiritual strugglers, as His soldiers, we enjoy the eternal feast, inheriting the glory that does not perish. As the Apostle says: "The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God: and if children, then heirs; heirs of God, and joint-heirs with Christ" (Rom 8:16-17).

3 And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews. 4 Then the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther. So Esther arose, and stood before the king. If Mordecai received the king's seal as a sign of enjoying the eternal feast, then Esther enjoyed appearing before the king; this appearing in his presence is the true "feast", where the Church enjoys the companionship of God, His dwelling within her, and her entrance into His bosom.

The Scripture says: "And Esther spake yet again before the king, and fell down at his feet, and besought him with tears to put away the mischief of Haman the Agagite, and his device that he had devised against the Jews. Then the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther. So Esther arose, and stood before the king" [3-4].

The true feast is a meeting with the Lord or a standing before Him; it is a rising after a fall, as the Scripture says of Esther: "fell down at his feet... Then the king held out the golden sceptre toward Esther. So Esther arose...". In other words, the feast is an entrance into the experience of the Resurrection through the Cross (the golden scepter).

May we go with Esther to the King, and in contrition declare our fall at His feet, that we may weep with her and plead because of the bitterness of the devil's schemes against us, so that the Lord may stretch out His hand through His heavenly, life-giving Cross, and we may rise and be found with Him eternally.

entries.section: 4. The issuing of the new royal decree:

paragraphs.text: 5 And said, If it please the king, and if I have found favour in his sight, and the thing seem right before the king, and I be pleasing in his eyes, let it be written to reverse the letters devised by Haman the son of Hammedatha the Agagite, which he wrote to destroy the Jews which are in all the king's provinces: 6 For how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people? or how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred? 7 Then the king Ahasuerus said unto Esther the queen and to Mordecai the Jew, Behold, I have given Esther the house of Haman, and him they have hanged upon the gallows, because he laid his hand upon the Jews. 8 Write ye also for the Jews, as it liketh you, in the king's name, and seal it with the king's ring: for the writing which is written in the king's name, and sealed with the king's ring, may no man reverse. 9 Then were the king's scribes called at that time in the third month, that is, the month Sivan, on the three and twentieth day thereof; and it was written according to all that Mordecai commanded unto the Jews, and to the lieutenants, and the deputies and rulers of the provinces which are from India unto Ethiopia, an hundred twenty and seven provinces, unto every province according to the writing thereof, and unto every people after their language, and to the Jews according to their writing, and according to their language. 10 And he wrote in the king Ahasuerus' name, and sealed it with the king's ring, and sent letters by posts on horseback, and riders on mules, camels, and young dromedaries: 11 Wherein the king granted the Jews which were in every city to gather themselves together, and to stand for their life, to destroy, to slay, and to cause to perish, all the power of the people and province that would assault them, both little ones and women, and to take the spoil of them for a prey, 12 Upon one day in all the provinces of king Ahasuerus, namely, upon the thirteenth day of the twelfth month, which is the month Adar. 13 The copy of the writing for a commandment to be given in every province was published unto all people, and that the Jews should be ready against that day to avenge themselves on their enemies. 14 So the posts that rode upon mules and camels went out, being hastened and pressed on by the king's commandment. And the decree was given at Shushan the palace.

Through Haman the first decree was issued, in which was the sentence of death; and now through Mordecai and Esther, through Esther's banquet, that is, the banquet of the Cross, the first decree was torn up (Col 2:15) and a new decree was issued on our behalf, in which our sonship to God and the destruction of our enemies (the devil and his hosts) are proclaimed.

entries.section: 4. The issuing of the new royal decree:

paragraphs.text: How beautiful are the words of Esther (the Church) to the king as she intercedes for her people: "For how can I endure to see the evil that shall come unto my people? or how can I endure to see the destruction of my kindred?" [6]. These are the feelings of the Church toward every soul, the feelings of shepherds and flock alike, for all are aflame with the love of the salvation of others. These feelings took shape in the words of St. John Chrysostom, who never ceased to pray and labor for the salvation of every soul. Among his words: [Nothing is dearer to me than you, no, not even the light! I would gladly give my eyes tens of thousands of times and more, if possible, for the repentance of your souls. Your salvation is very dear to me, more than the light itself...! For what good are the rays of the sun to me if sorrow darkens my eyes because of you...?! What hope will I have if you do not progress?! And on the contrary, what despair can enter me as long as you are growing?! For when I hear joyful news about you I seem to have grown wings... You wipe away my sorrow! This is the whole burden of my prayers: I long for your growth... I love you, to the point of melting into you, and you are everything to me, my father and my mother, my brothers and my children].
Through this love which Mordecai and Esther showed, the new royal decree was issued, and its text is given in the Additions to Esther (Add. Esth 16), in which we find:

First: the condemnation of Haman as proud: "Many, the more often they are honored with the great bounty of their gracious princes, the more proud they become" (Add. Esth 16:2). In the former edict Ahasuerus regarded Haman as a father to him, and now he condemns him as proud. So when we fall into sin we regard the enemy as a father, but after the banquet of the Cross his true nature is exposed as a proud creature who abused the gift God gave him.

Second: the king reckoned that what had befallen the people had befallen him personally (Add. Esth 16:3-12) and that Haman had wished to deceive the great men and the rulers whom the king had set up. So by the Cross the Lord reckons every attack of the devil upon us and every deception as directed against His own kingdom, touching God Himself because we are His.

Third: he called the people: "the children of the most high, the most mighty, the living God, who by His kindness gave the kingdom to our fathers and to us, and has kept it until today" (Add. Esth 16:16). Thus through the events the pagan king touched the hand of God, and the trial became a mystery of blessing, so that many abandoned idolatry and believed in the living God. If the Jews were saved from extermination in the flesh, many of the pagans were saved from the death of idol worship.

15 And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a garment of fine linen and purple: and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad. 16 The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour. 17 And in every province, and in every city, whithersoever the king's commandment and his decree came, the Jews had joy and gladness, a feast and a good day. And many of the people of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews fell upon them.

"And Mordecai went out from the presence of the king in royal apparel of blue and white, and with a great crown of gold, and with a garment of fine linen and purple: and the city of Shushan rejoiced and was glad" [15].

It would not have been possible for the city of Shushan to put off the garments of mourning and enter into a life of exultation and joy unless Mordecai were first glorified before the king and clothed with the royal apparel, the golden crown and the garment of fine linen and purple. So the Church could not have enjoyed heavenly exultation and spiritual joy unless her Bridegroom, Christ Jesus, were glorified and raised to His Father. As He emptied Himself for our sake, so for our sake He was also glorified, that He might glorify us with Him, and we might put on with Him the royal apparel of blue and white, that is, the heavenly (blue) and pure (white) garment. In Christ Jesus we become kings (Rev 1:6) and put on the heavenly nature filled with purity. Through Him we also enjoy the heavenly (golden) crown, and put on the royal garment of righteousness (fine linen) (purple is the garment of kings).

When Mordecai was glorified, "The Jews had light, and gladness, and joy, and honour... And many of the people of the land became Jews; for the fear of the Jews fell upon them" [16-17]. So when the Lord Christ was glorified with the glory that He has from eternity, the Church enjoys light, that is, enlightenment, joy of the Spirit and inward honor...

Here, as the Church is glorified by the glorified Christ, we recall the dream that Mordecai saw in the Additions to Esther and its interpretation (Add. Esth 10-11). Mordecai saw voices and tumult, thunders and earthquakes on the earth, and behold, two great dragons were ready to fight, and the nations were stirred up, and the righteous cried out to God, and a little spring grew into a great river and overflowed with many waters, and then was transformed into light and sun. What are these voices but the voices of the Law and the types of the Old Testament that preceded the coming of the Word, to proclaim the spiritual warfare that exists not between Haman and Mordecai (the two great dragons) but between Satan and the Lord Christ; and this little spring, which is Esther, which became great for the people and became light and sun, signifies the Church, which went forth through the Lord Christ, who by His Incarnation humbled Himself and became like a little spring, so that He might overflow upon us with His Holy Spirit and shine in us with the splendor of His divinity, as the light of the world and the Sun of righteousness.

The dream carried an interpretation of the events of salvation in the days of Esther, and it carried a symbolic interpretation of the events of the true salvation accomplished by the Lord Christ Himself.

entries.section: 1. The victory and dominion of the Jews:

paragraphs.text: 1 Now in the twelfth month, that is, the month Adar, on the thirteenth day of the same, when the king's commandment and his decree drew near to be put in execution, in the day that the enemies of the Jews hoped to have power over them, (though it was turned to the contrary, that the Jews had rule over them that hated them;) 2 The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, to lay hand on such as sought their hurt: and no man could withstand them; for the fear of them fell upon all people. 3 And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them. 4 For Mordecai was great in the king's house, and his fame went out throughout all the provinces: for this man Mordecai waxed greater and greater. 5 Thus the Jews smote all their enemies with the stroke of the sword, and slaughter, and destruction, and did what they would unto those that hated them. 6 And in Shushan the palace the Jews slew and destroyed five hundred men. 7 And Parshandatha, and Dalphon, and Aspatha, 8 And Poratha, and Adalia, and Aridatha, 9 And Parmashta, and Arisai, and Aridai, and Vajezatha, 10 The ten sons of Haman the son of Hammedatha, the enemy of the Jews, slew they; but on the spoil laid they not their hand.

entries.section: 1. The victory and dominion of the Jews:

paragraphs.text: Two royal edicts reached all the provinces. One was sent by Haman from Shushan the palace, dated the thirteenth of the first month, demanding the killing and extermination of the Jews. The second was sent by Mordecai, also from Shushan the palace, dated the twenty-third of the third month, authorizing the Jews to draw the sword against their enemies in defense of themselves. When the thirteenth day of the twelfth month came, the enemies of the Jews resolved to fight them on the basis of the first edict, while the Jews relied on the second edict and rose to fight them, and the Lord gave them awe, for "no man could withstand them; for the fear of them fell upon all people. And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants, and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them" [2-3].

Although the enemy (the devil) rages against the Church, yet where he thinks he is able to prevail, he is defeated under her feet, as the Lord Himself says: "the gates of hell shall not prevail against it" (Mt 16:18), and as He says to the Church in Philadelphia: "Behold, I will make them of the synagogue of Satan, which say they are Jews, and are not, but do lie; behold, I will make them to come and worship before thy feet, and to know that I have loved thee" (Rev 3:9).

entries.section: 1. The victory and dominion of the Jews:

paragraphs.text: Haman prepared the gallows for Mordecai and was hanged on it, and his ten sons were also hanged [14], and since he devised the complete extermination of the people, all his followers perished!

The enemies began to oppose the Jews although they knew of the second edict, and wanted to gain dominion over them [1]; they attacked them, and all allied together to harm them [2], and that brought about their own shame. Jewish tradition says that no one stood against this people at that time except the Amalekites, whose hearts were hardened like Pharaoh's, and the sons of Haman were determined to avenge their father's blood at whatever cost.

The Scripture says: "The Jews gathered themselves together in their cities throughout all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, to lay hand on such as sought their hurt: and no man could withstand them; for the fear of them fell upon all people" [2].

This collective movement carries a spiritual meaning that touches our life in the Lord. The gathering of the Jews in their cities throughout all the provinces of the king signifies the consecration of all the senses of man, his impulses and his energies, each gift in its place, so long as it is in the provinces of the king, that is, subject to the Kingdom of God, so that all of them work together with one spirit and one mind to resist the devil with all his thoughts and enticements, which are an enmity seeking to harm us. Thus no man can withstand us, that is, no sin can have dominion over us so long as all that is in us belongs to the Lord, and we become in the eyes of the devil awesome and terrifying to him.

The account continues thus: "And all the rulers of the provinces, and the lieutenants (the stewards), and the deputies, and officers of the king, helped the Jews; because the fear of Mordecai fell upon them" [3].

The Jews gathered to act with one spirit and so were terrifying to the enemy, and the officials also supported them because of the awe of Mordecai. I say that this is a picture of spiritual striving. The gathering of the Jews in their cities, as I said, signifies the stirring up of the senses and inward energies for spiritual striving through a life of sanctification, while the rulers, stewards, deputies and officers of the king signify the outward support of man, such as the help of the heavenly orders, the company of the saints who have fallen asleep in the Lord and the prayers of those who are striving... For the person who lives in the Lord carries strength within him and also help through the holy company, whether of those who have fallen asleep or of those who are striving; therefore the Apostle says: "Wherefore seeing we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses, let us lay aside every weight, and the sin which doth so easily beset us, and let us run with patience the race that is set before us" (Heb 12:1).

Since the people carried the power of the Spirit and its unity within, and divine support from without, they struck their enemies... The number of the slain in Shushan the palace reached five hundred men, and the ten sons of Haman were also killed... And the people did not lay their hand on the spoil, although the king had allowed them to do so (Esth 8:11). Perhaps they wanted to confirm their intention before all, that they did not covet material gain nor use the king's edict to achieve private aims, but sought only their deliverance. For this reason also they did not kill the children and women, although they had been permitted to do so (Esth 8:11).

11 On that day the number of those that were slain in Shushan the palace was brought before the king. 12 And the king said unto Esther the queen, The Jews have slain and destroyed five hundred men in Shushan the palace, and the ten sons of Haman; what have they done in the rest of the king's provinces? now what is thy petition? and it shall be granted thee: or what is thy request further? and it shall be done. 13 Then said Esther, If it please the king, let it be granted to the Jews which are in Shushan to do to morrow also according unto this day's decree, and let Haman's ten sons be hanged upon the gallows. 14 And the king commanded it so to be done: and the decree was given at Shushan; and they hanged Haman's ten sons. 15 For the Jews that were in Shushan gathered themselves together on the fourteenth day also of the month Adar, and slew three hundred men at Shushan; but on the prey they laid not their hand. 16 But the other Jews that were in the king's provinces gathered themselves together, and stood for their lives, and had rest from their enemies, and slew of their foes seventy and five thousand, but they laid not their hands on the prey, 17 On the thirteenth day of the month Adar; and on the fourteenth day of the same rested they, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. 18 But the Jews that were at Shushan assembled together on the thirteenth day thereof, and on the fourteenth thereof; and on the fifteenth day of the same they rested, and made it a day of feasting and gladness. 19 Therefore the Jews of the villages, that dwelt in the unwalled towns, made the fourteenth day of the month Adar a day of gladness and feasting, and a good day, and of sending portions one to another.

When the king presented to Esther the number of the slain in Shushan the palace (five hundred men and the ten sons of Haman), she asked him to allow them to kill their enemies on the following day as well, and to hang the sons of Haman on the gallows. Esther did not ask this out of love of bloodshed, but perhaps she realized that the enemy was still devising plans to make Haman's plan succeed, so she wanted to put an end to the matter, while the hanging of Haman's sons was to be a warning to anyone who might be tempted to devise evil.

In any case, what Esther did signifies the believer's obligation to strike the works of the devil to the end, leaving no remnant of him inside the palace (the heart), lest the enemy rise again and fight the soul anew. Let us cut off from the palace of our inner life every root of sin, so that the palace may be holy for the Lord.
This was with regard to Shushan the palace; but as for all the provinces, they kept to the king's decision that the vengeance should be on the thirteenth day alone, and no other day was given.

20 And Mordecai wrote these things, and sent letters unto all the Jews that were in all the provinces of the king Ahasuerus, both nigh and far, 21 To stablish this among them, that they should keep the fourteenth day of the month Adar, and the fifteenth day of the same, yearly, 22 As the days wherein the Jews rested from their enemies, and the month which was turned unto them from sorrow to joy, and from mourning into a good day: that they should make them days of feasting and joy, and of sending portions one to another, and gifts to the poor. 23 And the Jews undertook to do as they had begun, and as Mordecai had written unto them; 24 Because Haman the son of Hammedatha, the Agagite, the enemy of all the Jews, had devised against the Jews to destroy them, and had cast Pur, that is, the lot, to consume them, and to destroy them; 25 But when Esther came before the king, he commanded by letters that his wicked device, which he devised against the Jews, should return upon his own head, and that he and his sons should be hanged on the gallows. 26 Wherefore they called these days Purim after the name of Pur. Therefore for all the words of this letter, and of that which they had seen concerning this matter, and which had come unto them, 27 The Jews ordained, and took upon them, and upon their seed, and upon all such as joined themselves unto them, so as it should not fail, that they would keep these two days according to their writing, and according to their appointed time every year; 28 And that these days should be remembered and kept throughout every generation, every family, every province, and every city; and that these days of Purim should not fail from among the Jews, nor the memorial of them perish from their seed. 29 Then Esther the queen, the daughter of Abihail, and Mordecai the Jew, wrote with all authority, to confirm this second letter of Purim. 30 And he sent the letters unto all the Jews, to the hundred twenty and seven provinces of the kingdom of Ahasuerus, with words of peace and truth, 31 To confirm these days of Purim in their times appointed, according as Mordecai the Jew and Esther the queen had enjoined them, and as they had decreed for themselves and for their seed, the matters of the fastings and their cry. 32 And the decree of Esther confirmed these matters of Purim; and it was written in the book.

Mordecai sent to all the Jews in all the provinces belonging to the kingdom of Persia that they should celebrate on the fourteenth and fifteenth days of the month of Adar every year, as a remembrance of the Lord's work with them, and that they should give gifts and donations to the poor. For as the Lord cared for them and saved their lives, each one should care for his neighbor and not ignore the poor and needy... This feast was called the "Feast of Purim". We have already spoken about its ritual.

Esther also sent, together with Mordecai, confirming the necessity of celebrating the feast as a hymn of thanksgiving to God, who works on behalf of His children. As St. Jerome says: [Esther, a type of the Church, delivered her people from danger, and having slain Haman, whose name means "injustice", she handed down to the generations a memorial day and a great feast].

1 And the king Ahasuerus laid a tribute upon the land, and upon the isles of the sea. 2 And all the acts of his power and of his might, and the declaration of the greatness of Mordecai, whereunto the king advanced him, are they not written in the book of the chronicles of the kings of Media and Persia? 3 For Mordecai the Jew was next unto king Ahasuerus, and great among the Jews, and accepted of the multitude of his brethren, seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed.

This chapter presents to us a picture of the greatness of Ahasuerus, to whom many provinces submitted and paid tribute, and of Mordecai, the second man, "great among the Jews, and accepted of the multitude of his brethren, seeking the wealth of his people, and speaking peace to all his seed" [3]. The secret of his greatness was the breadth of his heart in love for his brethren and his speaking of peace for the sake of his children. He became a source of blessing for his generation and for the coming generations through his surpassing love.
If the whole people were glorified by their deliverance from the enemy, Mordecai, who sought not what was his own but what belonged to others, was glorified more and more.

In the Additions to Esther this chapter continues with a review of Mordecai's dream, in which God assured him that He was working through him and Esther for the salvation of their brethren; we have already spoken about this dream.
Our good God, who gave Esther and Mordecai the grace of an open mouth and a heart enlarged with love for their brethren, opens our hearts for the edification of every soul, to the glory of God!
* You will find the commentaries on the remaining chapters of the book in the commentary of Fr. Antonious Fikry on the Book of Esther.
